question: The original statue of this creature was sculpted by Lim Nang Seng and unveiled in 1972 by Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew. Alec Fraser-Brunner, the curator of the Van Kleef Aquarium, designed it in 1964 as a logo for the Singapore Tourist Promotion Board. The main statue stands 8.6 metres tall, weighs about 70 tonnes, and spouts water from its mouth. Its fish body represents Singapore's origins as a fishing village called Temasek. For 10 points, name this Singaporean mascot with the head of a lion and the body of a fish.

This resort was designed by the architect Moshe Safdie and developed by an American casino company. It opened in 2010 and includes a casino. Its three hotel towers are each about 55 storeys tall. They are topped by a platform 340 metres long that cantilevers out over one end, with a 150-metre infinity pool. For 10 points, name this Singapore hotel and casino resort whose rooftop SkyPark overlooks the city skyline.
answer: Marina Bay Sands [or MBS; prompt on "Marina Bay" or "Sands"]

question: This dish is believed to have evolved from a specialty of Wenchang, on an island in southern China. Immigrants from that island brought it to Southeast Asia in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The bird is poached whole at a gentle heat, and the stock is kept. The grain is fried in the bird's fat, then cooked in that stock with ginger, garlic and pandan leaves. For 10 points, name this dish, served with chilli sauce, dark soy sauce and cucumber, that is called one of Singapore's national dishes.
answer: Hainanese chicken rice [prompt on "chicken" or "rice"; accept Hainanese chicken rice]

question: This island's former name has been translated as the island behind which lies death. Fort Siloso, one of several British forts built here in the late nineteenth century, guarded the harbour entrance. During the Second World War it held a prisoner-of-war camp. In 2018 the Capella hotel here hosted a summit between Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un. For 10 points, name this resort island off Singapore's southern coast that is home to Universal Studios Singapore and whose Malay name means peace and tranquillity.

This man studied law at Cambridge and was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1950. He co-founded the People's Action Party in 1954 with colleagues including Goh Keng Swee and Toh Chin Chye. He became prime minister in 1959 at the age of 35 and held the office until 1990, then served as Senior Minister and Minister Mentor until 2011. He died on 23 March 2015, and one of his sons later also became prime minister. For 10 points, name this longtime prime minister of Singapore.
answer: Lee Kuan Yew [or LKY; prompt on "Lee"; do not accept or prompt on "Lee Hsien Loong"]

question: This man was born in 1781 aboard his father's ship off the coast of Jamaica. He served as Lieutenant-Governor of Java and later of Bencoolen, and wrote a two-volume history of Java. He was the first president of the Zoological Society of London. He is commemorated by a marble sculpture by Francis Chantrey in Westminster Abbey, though he is buried at Hendon. For 10 points, name this British official who landed on 29 January 1819 and founded a settlement on the island of Singapore.

Linguists debate how much of this word comes from Malay, Hokkien and Cantonese, all of which have a similar sentence-final particle. It is one of the discourse particles of Colloquial Singapore English, alongside lor, leh, meh and hor. The Oxford English Dictionary added it in the year 2000. That was also the year the Speak Good English Movement was launched to discourage the variety of English in which it appears. For 10 points, give this one-syllable particle that ends many sentences in Singlish.

This athlete attended Anglo-Chinese School before enrolling at the University of Texas at Austin, where he was coached by Eddie Reese. At the 2015 SEA Games he broke a 33-year-old national record in the 50 metre freestyle. He received a S$1 million award from his government under its Multi-Million Dollar Award Programme. On 12 August 2016 he won the 100 metre butterfly in an Olympic record time, beating the mark set by Michael Phelps in 2008. For 10 points, name this swimmer who won his country's first Olympic gold medal in Rio de Janeiro.

The main road here was renamed from Reformatory Road in 1947 after a governor of the Straits Settlements, though historians disagree about which one. During the Japanese invasion of 1942, that road was one of the defence lines of the Malay Regiment in the Battle of Pasir Panjang. The Housing and Development Board built its eighth planned estate here between 1975 and 1979, partly on the site of Colombo Camp. Ngee Ann Polytechnic is located here, and its East-West Line station has the code EW23. For 10 points, name this district in western Singapore, between Jurong East and Dover on the MRT.

The recipe for this cocktail was reportedly lost after the 1930s and reconstructed from a note written by a visitor in 1936. Its ingredients include cherry liqueur, Benedictine, pineapple juice, lime juice, grenadine and Angostura bitters. It is traditionally credited to Ngiam Tong Boon, a bartender who created it in 1915 at the Long Bar of a famous colonial-era hotel. Its pink colour was meant to make it look like fruit juice, so that women could drink alcohol in public. For 10 points, name this pink cocktail, served in a hurricane glass and named for a Southeast Asian city-state.

A retaining wall collapsed on 20 April 2004 at a tunnel site near the Merdeka Bridge, killing four workers and delaying the opening of this line. Its Stage 3, from Bartley to Marymount, opened on 28 May 2009. It is the fourth line on its country's MRT network and is operated by SMRT Trains. It runs fully automated, three-car Alstom Metropolis trains controlled by the Urbalis signalling system. For 10 points, name this orange-coloured, driverless, orbital MRT line that links Singapore's radial lines.

A causeway across the Johor Strait was blown up on 31 January to slow the advance that led to this event. Japanese troops crossed the strait on 8 February and attacked the weakly defended northwest of the island. On the morning of 15 February, Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival met eleven senior officers in the Battlebox, where they noted that less than 24 hours of water remained. That evening Percival signed an unconditional capitulation to General Tomoyuki Yamashita in the boardroom of the Ford Factory. For 10 points, name this February 1942 capitulation that Winston Churchill called the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history and that led to more than three years of Japanese rule over the island.
answer: Fall of Singapore [or Battle of Singapore or Surrender of Singapore]

question: A file code-named Albatross, declassified in recent years, shows that this event was a negotiated decision rather than a sudden ejection. Finance Minister Goh Keng Swee proposed it to Tun Razak in July 1965. It followed communal riots in 1964 and the People's Action Party's decision to contest the federal election, in which it won just one seat. The federal Parliament approved it by a vote of 126 to 0, and Tunku Abdul Rahman announced it on 9 August 1965. For 10 points, name this event, two years after a merger, in which Singapore left Malaysia and became a sovereign state.
answer: separation of Singapore from Malaysia [or Singapore's expulsion from Malaysia or expulsion of Singapore from Malaysia; or independence of Singapore; accept word forms]

question: A 1990 parliamentary speech warned that ministers should not be infected by a "syndrome" of this word. It began as slang among conscripts doing National Service. It comes from a Hokkien expression whose Chinese characters mean afraid to lose. The Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2007 and made it a Word of the Day in 2015. For 10 points, give this Singlish adjective for a competitive fear of missing out, as in a parent who queues overnight for a school place.
answer: kiasu [or kiasuism or kiasuness; accept word forms; do not accept or prompt on "kiasi"]

question: Members of this community traditionally spoke a creole of Malay with Hokkien vocabulary that is now dying out. The women wore the kebaya and beaded slippers called kasut manik. Their cuisine features Malay spices in dishes such as laksa and ayam buah keluak. Their origins are traced to traders who settled in Malacca and married local women. For 10 points, name this community descended from those traders in Malacca, Penang and Singapore, whose name comes from a Malay word for child.
answer: Peranakan [or Peranakan Chinese; or Straits Chinese; or Baba-Nyonya; or Baba and Nyonya]

question: A Chinese traveller named Wang Dayuan visited around 1330 and described two settlements here, Long Ya Men and Ban Zu. He recorded that a Siamese attack a few years earlier had failed to take the fortified city after a month. The Javanese poem Nagarakretagama, written in 1365, also mentions the place. The name likely derives from a Malay word for sea or lake. For 10 points, give this 14th-century name, meaning sea town, for the settlement on the site of modern Singapore, which was later replaced by a name meaning Lion City and is now borne by a sovereign wealth fund.
answer: Temasek [or Tumasik or Tamasak or Danmaxi; prompt on "Singapura"; do not accept "Singapore"]

question: The composer of this piece was born in Bukittinggi in 1907 and wrote about 1,500 songs, including the song Semoga Bahagia. It was commissioned in 1958 by the City Council's deputy mayor, Ong Pang Boon, and first performed on 6 September 1958 at the reopening of the Victoria Theatre. In 2001 an official relaunch lowered its key from G major to F major. By law it may be sung only in Malay, though authorised translations exist in English, Mandarin and Tamil. For 10 points, name this piece by Zubir Said, the country's national anthem, whose title is an exhortation to the country.

Colonel Masanobu Tsuji served as chief of planning for this operation, which General Tomoyuki Yamashita commanded. Its victims were killed at sites including Changi Beach, Punggol Point and Tanah Merah. The selection was arbitrary, and people were condemned for wearing glasses or having tattoos. Estimates of the toll vary widely, from under 5,000 in Japanese records to at least 50,000 in Singaporean ones. For 10 points, name this massacre of ethnic Chinese carried out from 18 February to 4 March 1942, whose Chinese name means purge through cleansing.
answer: Sook Ching [or Operation Sook Ching; or Sook Ching massacre; or Kakyo Shukusei]

question: A judge named Algernon Brown declared a marriage void in December 1950, one solemnised when the bride was 13 to a 21-year-old man named Mansoor Adabi. The bride had been born in Tjimahi, Java, in 1937 and was given in 1943 to Che Aminah binte Mohamed, who raised her as a Muslim in Kemaman, Terengganu. After the judge awarded custody to her Dutch parents, photographs of the girl kneeling before a statue of the Virgin Mary inflamed Muslim opinion. The unrest lasted from 11 to 13 December, leaving 18 dead and 173 injured. For 10 points, name these 1950 disturbances in Singapore sparked by a custody battle over a Dutch-born girl.
answer: Maria Hertogh riots [or Natrah riots or Nadra riots; prompt on "Maria Hertogh" or "Natrah" or "Nadra"]

question: A Japanese-built fishing boat named Kofuku Maru was renamed after a small but deadly Asian snake for this operation. It sailed from Exmouth, Western Australia, on 1 September 1943. On the night of 26 September, six commandos in three folding canoes attached limpet mines to Japanese ships in Singapore Harbour. The Japanese blamed local saboteurs, leading to the Double Tenth incident of mass arrests, torture and executions. For 10 points, name this 1943 raid by Z Special Unit commandos led by Ivan Lyon, which was followed a year later by Operation Rimau.
answer: Operation Jaywick [prompt on "Krait" or "MV Krait"; do not accept "Operation Rimau"]

question: This word comes from a term for an official stamp used to authenticate documents, borrowed from Hindi by way of colonial-era Malay. The practice it names works purely by social consensus, since nothing in law gives the marker any power to hold a space. It has since spread from tables to other spots, such as parking spaces and places in a queue. In Singapore's hawker centres it is done by leaving a small object, most often a pocket packet of tissues, on a seat. For 10 points, give this Singlish verb meaning to reserve a seat while you go and queue for food.

The name of this food in Singapore comes from an Indian word, and the same food has a different name in Malaysia that derives from the Malay for rolling dough thinly. The dough is made from flour, water and fat, usually ghee, and is repeatedly kneaded, oiled and folded to create layers. It is stretched paper-thin, gathered into a rope, wound into a spiral, flattened and cooked on an oiled griddle. Variants include a paper-thin sugary one served with condensed milk, a thick one stuffed with eggs, meat and onions called murtabak, and ones filled with egg or onion. For 10 points, name this South Indian-derived flatbread, eaten with curry or dal for breakfast in Singapore.
answer: roti prata [or prata or roti canai or canai; prompt on "roti" or "paratha" or "parotta"]

question: A man who reaches this milestone stops being a full-time conscript and becomes a part-time one. Under a law passed on 14 March 1967, male citizens and second-generation permanent residents are liable, and full-time service used to last two and a half years rather than two. Afterwards he serves for ten years, with up to 40 days of training a year, until age 40, or 50 for commissioned officers. It applies in the army, navy, police and civil defence force. For 10 points, give this three-letter acronym for the day National Service men count down to, which they celebrate by shouting it followed by a familiar Hokkien particle.

This place began in the late 1800s as Chan Chu Kang Village, before being renamed for a wealthy businessman and community leader. Block 101 in its oldest neighbourhood, Chong Pang, was the first public housing block built here, and a multiplex here that opened in 1992 as Singapore's first was designed to resemble a rocket ship. Its present name is the Mandarin pinyin form of the dialect name of a man surnamed Lim, who made a fortune from rubber and pineapple plantations, and it was adopted in the 1980s. Its reputation for strange news made it the source of Singapore's version of Florida Man memes, and Netflix made a Stranger Things promotional short film set in it. For 10 points, name this North Region district, home to Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, that lies between Sembawang and Ang Mo Kio.

This assessment was first held in 1960 and was modelled on the British eleven-plus. Ties in it for placement are broken by citizenship, then by the order in which a family ranked its education choices, and finally by a computerised ballot run by the Ministry of Education. Until 2020 it was scored by a T-score with about 300 possible values, but since 2021 the total is the sum of four subject bands numbered from 1 to 8, giving a range from 4 to 32. It tests English, a mother tongue such as Chinese, Malay or Tamil, mathematics and science. For 10 points, name this nationwide assessment taken near the end of pupils' sixth year, before they move on to secondary education.
answer: PSLE [or Primary School Leaving Examination or Primary School Leaving Exam]

question: Negotiations for the U.S.-Singapore free trade agreement led Singapore to relax this rule in 2004, after the Wrigley Company lobbied for a change. The exception covers sugar-free therapeutic and dental products with calcium lactate, and nicotine varieties, which can be sold only by doctors or pharmacists. Selling the item carries fines of up to S$2,000, though simply possessing it is legal. The rule took effect on 3 January 1992, after vandals stuck the item on the door sensors of MRT trains, which had opened in 1987, and on mailboxes, keyholes and lift buttons. For 10 points, name this Singaporean prohibition on selling and importing a sticky confection that people blow into bubbles.
answer: chewing gum ban [or gum ban or ban on chewing gum or chewing gum sales ban; prompt on "chewing gum" or "gum"]

question: This programme ran on MediaCorp Channel 5 from 25 September 1997 to 11 February 2007, over eight seasons and 166 episodes. Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong voiced concern over its liberal use of Singlish, and by its third season the dialogue was adapted to limit it. Its lead, played by Gurmit Singh, wears yellow boots bought at Beach Road, and has curly hair, a black mole and long pinky fingernails. His wife Rosie is played by Irene Ang, and his sister-in-law Margaret is played by Tan Kheng Hua. For 10 points, name this Singaporean sitcom about an Ah Beng contractor who says Use your brain and Don't play play.
answer: Phua Chu Kang [or Phua Chu Kang Pte Ltd or PCK; prompt on "Phua"]

question: Wiktionary lists documented uses of a shortened form of this expression in Usenet posts and in books about Singapore culture, from 1996 to 2015. Its first syllable alone can be used to curse at someone, to express disappointment or to show anger, much as English profanities do. In Singapore it is used in colloquial English to express dismay or disapproval, and it is common in Hong Kong too. Its language was one of those targeted by the Speak Mandarin Campaign, which Lee Kuan Yew launched on 7 September 1979, and the last television programmes in that language were phased out in 1981. For 10 points, name this vulgar four-syllable expletive from a dialect associated with Hong Kong and Guangzhou.
answer: diu lei lou mo [or diu nei lo mo or diu lay lou mou or diu lei or diu nei]

question: The Eurodance song Million Tears became the unofficial anthem of this group. A 2003 Singaporean film, 15, referenced it, though direct mentions of it were edited out. Originally open only to Chinese members, it relaxed that rule in the 1970s and recruited Malay and Indian members, partly through connections made at disco tea dances. Its name is a string of numbers whose sum is 18, a nod to an older gang, the Eighteen Arhats. For 10 points, name this Singaporean secret society, active since the 1970s, whose Hokkien name is made of digits.
answer: Salakau [or Sah Lak Kau or Sa Lak Kau or 369 or three six nine]

question: In December 2016 this person fled to the United States, and a judge granted political asylum on 24 March 2017 after finding that he faced persecution for his political opinions in Singapore. He was sentenced on 6 July 2015 to four weeks in prison, with three weeks for wounding religious feelings and one week for an obscene image. He was found guilty on 12 May 2015 of offences under Sections 298 and 292 of the Penal Code. The charges came from a video, posted on 27 March 2015 when he was 16, which compared Lee Kuan Yew with Jesus. For 10 points, name this Singaporean YouTuber, prosecuted after making a video in the days following the death of the country's first prime minister.

In Singapore this item is worn mainly by men of the Sikh community, who keep the hair it covers uncut as a gift from their Guru. Wearers who worked as night watchmen were called jaga, guarding banks, warehouses and homes across the colonial city. The earliest Sikhs to wear it in Singapore likely arrived soon after 1819, working as sepoys, servants or convicts for the British East India Company. Singapore's 2010 census counted just under 13,000 Sikhs, most tracing their heritage to Punjab. For 10 points, name this wrapped cloth headdress covering long, uncut hair.

This surname derives from the Sanskrit word for lion and was traditionally used by Rajput warriors before the tenth Sikh guru mandated it for every initiated Sikh man. He introduced it at the founding of the Khalsa on Baisakhi in 1699, pairing it with the surname Kaur for women so that caste could no longer be read from a name. In Singapore, men bearing it formed the Sikh Police Contingent, established in 1881 and disbanded at the end of World War Two. It remains the surname shared by nearly all Sikh men in Singapore today, though bearers need not be related, since it functions as a shared identity rather than a family lineage. For 10 points, give this one-word surname, also a common given name across Punjabi and wider Indian society, that literally means lion.

This institution began in 1963 as an independent college with just 116 students, funded by a Teochew clan association founded in 1845 by the businessman Seah Eu Chin. Its name comes from the old name for Chaozhou, the ancestral home of many of its Teochew founders. It was renamed a technical college in 1968 when its founding kongsi transferred management to the government, before taking its current name in April 1982. Its main campus sits on 33.6 hectares in Clementi, near the fringe of Bukit Timah. For 10 points, name this Singaporean tertiary institution named after a Teochew charitable organization.

This institution opened on 3 January 1977 at a campus in Dover with 968 students, established after Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew's 1970 offer of a dollar-for-dollar government grant to its founding school for a pre-university campus. That founding school was established at 70 Amoy Street on 1 March 1886 by the Methodist missionary William Fitzjames Oldham. It is one of several Singaporean schools founded by the same Methodist mission, alongside a same-named independent secondary school and one on Barker Road. For 10 points, give the four-letter abbreviation of this pre-university school in Dover.

Designed by the Japanese architect Toyo Ito, this building's rooftop was conceived as an active public space featuring an open-air amphitheatre, a wading pool and a landscaped Sky Park. Developed by a Temasek Holdings subsidiary for S$417 million, it had a soft opening on 7 October 2006 and an official opening on 1 December of that year. Spanning almost 100,000 square metres of net lettable area across three storeys and two basement levels, it is connected to a namesake MRT station and bus interchange. For 10 points, name this shopping mall in the HarbourFront precinct, for years the largest in Singapore.

This institution's oldest constituent traces to a medical school opened on 28 September 1905, which was renamed in 1913 after a reigning British monarch. That college merged with Raffles College, opened in 1929, to form an institution bearing Malaya's name in 1949. After that institution split, its island-based arm took the island's name in 1962, and its law faculty later spent 25 years at Kent Ridge before moving back to a Bukit Timah campus once occupied by Raffles College. On 8 August 1980, a merger with a Nanyang institution created its present form. For 10 points, name this institution, a major institution of higher learning in the city-state.

Immigrants installed a shrine to this deity between 1820 and 1824 at what is now the Fuk Tak Chi Temple, one of the earliest stops for Chinese arrivals in Singapore. He is usually depicted as a smiling old man with a white beard, and worship of him spread through temples serving Hakka, Cantonese, Hokkien and Teochew communities alike. A temple to him on Kusu Island was established in 1923 and marked its centenary in 2023. Devotees credit him with protection from illness and danger and know him as the God of Prosperity and Virtue. For 10 points, name this popular Chinese folk deity, whose Hokkien name literally means Grand Uncle.
answer: Tua Peh Kong [or Tua Pek Kong or Da Bo Gong]

question: In Singapore, the sole legal authority to certify this status belongs to Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura, a statutory body established in 1968 under the Administration of Muslim Law Act. Because food and other products made overseas cannot be certified by that body directly, Singapore instead recognizes a list of approved foreign certification bodies in each exporting country. From October 2025 a new digital certificate and a stricter framework for recognizing those foreign bodies took effect. Restaurants and food manufacturers display its certificate to show compliance with Islamic dietary law. For 10 points, give this Arabic word, the opposite of haram, that describes food permissible under Islamic law.

According to a widely repeated origin story, nineteenth-century Chinese coolies working at the Singapore River boiled pork bones with herbs, believing the resulting broth would restore their strength for manual labour. Its Hokkien name literally combines the words for meat, bone and tea, even though no tea leaves go into the pot itself. Singapore's dominant style is associated with Teochew immigrants and is a clear, peppery, garlicky broth, unlike the darker, herbal, soy-sauce-heavy version associated with Klang, Malaysia and often attributed to Hokkien immigrants. It is typically eaten with pork ribs, rice and a side of fried dough sticks. For 10 points, name this Singaporean and Malaysian pork rib soup dish.

This Hokkien-derived Singlish phrase combines a word meaning "cannot" or "not" with one meaning "pleased" or "satisfied." Used bluntly as a standalone interjection, it can carry the confrontational sense of "got a problem with that?" It usually describes low-level irritation rather than serious anger, the kind brought on by a long queue or a lost parking spot, and it can also describe being uncomfortable or disgusted rather than merely annoyed. Drop its negating first word and the remaining word instead describes something satisfying or a great feeling. For 10 points, give this two-word Singlish phrase for being unhappy or dissatisfied.

This expression is commonly abbreviated to three letters in both speech and text, and combined with a separate coarse Hokkien insult, it forms an even cruder six-letter compound abbreviation. Linguists trace it, like much Hokkien profanity, to a slur invoking the addressee's mother, though many younger speakers use it as a general-purpose intensifier akin to the English F-word rather than a literal insult. It appears throughout informal Singaporean speech and text, and lexicographers have catalogued it in Singlish reference works despite its extreme vulgarity. Most Chinese Singaporeans, apart from some rough-edged youths, consider it highly offensive. For 10 points, give this three-letter abbreviation of a crude Hokkien exclamation of anger or frustration.

This vulgar Singlish interjection is usually abbreviated to three letters, the second of which stands for a coarse slang term that is also a common standalone Hokkien insult. It expresses frustration or open contempt, often flung at someone considered especially foolish or unpleasant. Paired with a separate Hokkien profanity that invokes an addressee's mother, it forms an even cruder six-letter compound abbreviation. Reference works on Singlish document it as one of the most instantly recognizable vulgarities in Singapore's Hokkien-derived slang, despite, or because of, its extreme crudeness. For 10 points, give this three-letter abbreviation of a coarse Hokkien exclamation, often written out only in its abbreviated form.

This pair of near-synonymous Singlish terms both describe someone who shows off or acts boastfully. One, from Teochew, literally combines words for "good" and "face" and is loosely rendered as "loves to show off." The other, from Hokkien, literally translates to "fake smart" and specifically describes acting overly clever in a way that backfires into a rash, unwise decision. Both are common putdowns in Singapore's schoolyard and army slang, often used alongside the term kiasu, the fear of losing out. For 10 points, give either of these two Singlish terms for boastful or falsely clever behaviour.

In Singlish, this modal verb is a calque of the Hokkien word 會 or the Malay word "boleh," both meaning "able to" or "permitted to." Doubled around the word "is," it forms a stock phrase that either firmly reassure a listener that something is definitely doable, or hint that a plan, while theoretically possible, might not go as smoothly as hoped once put into practice. Newcomers are sometimes told that mastering this one doubled phrase is the fastest way to sound like a local. On its own, the single-syllable word already answers a yes-or-no question with a flat, confident affirmative, without needing a subject or full sentence. For 10 points, give this modal verb, repeated on both sides of "is" in a classic Singlish phrase of qualified affirmation.

This exclamation is generally traced to a Hokkien phrase literally meaning "my elder," though lexicographers dispute whether its second syllable clips a word for one's father or one's mother. Used mainly in Singapore and Malaysia, it can convey anything from mild annoyance to genuine shock, distress, or disbelief depending on tone and stress. It's often heard in a shorter two-syllable form, but gains an extra trailing syllable when spoken as its fuller, three-word version. A milder, near-synonymous exclamation, "alamak," is sometimes used interchangeably with it in casual conversation. For 10 points, give this Hokkien-derived exclamation of exasperation or surprise, whose longer form adds a final discourse particle.
answer: walao eh [or wah lau eh; accept walao or wah lau before "eh" is read]

question: This two-word phrase combines a Hokkien adjective meaning "crazy" with a particle that in Singlish marks a completed change of state, roughly equivalent to "already." Applied to a person, it can accuse them of behaving irrationally or acting out of their mind for no good reason. Applied instead to a situation, it expresses despair or resignation after something has gone badly wrong, similar to exclaiming "it's over" in English, as when someone realizes an assignment is due the next day and they haven't started. It's frequently paired with a preceding clause spelling out exactly what disaster has just occurred. For 10 points, give this Singlish phrase, literally "crazy already," used to lament a dire situation or accuse someone of madness.

Combining Hokkien words for "without" and "invite," this phrase is deployed as a mock-indignant complaint whenever someone posts evidence of an outing, meal, or event they weren't invited to. It functions as Singapore's ritualized shorthand for FOMO, appearing reflexively in the comments under a friend's Instagram food photo as a kind of scripted joke rather than a genuine grievance. Hokkien, brought to Singapore by immigrants from China's Fujian province, contributes many such loanwords to Singlish. The exchange typically runs the same way every time: someone posts, and friends flood the comments with this two-word accusation of exclusion. For 10 points, give this Hokkien-derived Singlish phrase literally meaning "no invite."

Borrowed from a Hokkien phrase literally meaning "to eat strength," or exhausting, this term broadened in Singlish into a general evaluation of a situation as severe, troublesome, or beyond ordinary inconvenience. Its Singlish spelling was influenced by Mandarin pinyin romanization despite its Hokkien origin. It can describe anything from unusually bad traffic to an unprepared student facing tomorrow's exam, functioning as an all-purpose intensifier for "this is bad." Locals might exclaim it upon realizing they've left an essential item at home just before a crucial appointment. For 10 points, give this Hokkien-derived Singlish term for a dire or troublesome situation.

The Oxford English Dictionary traces this word's earliest recorded English use to a 1977 issue of the Singapore newspaper New Nation. It likely entered Singaporean and Malaysian English from a Malay word meaning "pleasing" or "attractive," ultimately derived through Persian from Arabic, though some instead connect it to a Malay word for "enjoy," or note a coincidental resemblance to a Punjabi word for eagerness. It commonly describes food that's extremely delicious, an experience that's thoroughly satisfying, or occasionally a person considered highly attractive. For 10 points, give this exclamation of pleasure or approval, often shouted after a satisfying meal in Singapore.

The OED's earliest recorded use of this word as a noun comes from a 1993 issue of the publication Aliran Monthly. Borrowed from Malay, it describes idly loitering or hanging out with no particular purpose, and is especially associated with the leisure habits of younger generations in Singapore and Malaysia. It carries no negative connotation of laziness so much as a positive embrace of unstructured chilling out, often at a void deck, coffee shop, or park. Friends might invite each other to do this rather than plan anything more structured. For 10 points, give this Malay loanword for hanging out or relaxing idly.

A comment invoking this phrase beneath a Reddit post about an olive-green Uniqlo AIRism t-shirt that resembled an SAF uniform went viral among Singaporean commenters reminiscing about National Service. In its original military context, it's typically preceded by a complaint that "everybody in the company" is waiting on stragglers, before an instructor issues this command as a collective punishment. Hearing it means an entire platoon must instantly drop and assume the push-up position, regardless of individual fault. It's cited on lists of iconic quotes from BMT sergeants and enciks, alongside other blunt commands barked at slow-moving recruits. For 10 points, give this stock command that sends an entire Singapore Armed Forces unit into push-ups.
answer: whole lot knock it down [or equivalents like whole lot, knock it down]

question: Some purists restrict this phrase's rightful territory to only the strip between Kallang and Siglap, arguing that areas like Tampines and Pasir Ris don't really count despite lying in the same region of Singapore. Proponents of the saying often cite proximity to Changi Airport and a concentration of beloved hawker food as evidence for its truth. It expresses one half of a long-running rivalry over which half of the island is superior, playing out in constant online debate against a rival contingent centered on Jurong and the West. For 10 points, give this boastful catchphrase claiming the superiority of neighbourhoods such as Bedok and Katong.

Administered by five district agencies in the People's Association's network, this recurring payout was first rolled out in 2020 as targeted relief for lower-income households before evolving into a universal, digitalized transfer given to every Singaporean household regardless of income or housing type. Recipients split their allotment between hawkers and heartland merchants on one side and supermarkets on the other, with a combined 800 Singapore dollars disbursed across May 2025 and January 2026 alone. Named for the five district-level bodies that distribute it, it functions simultaneously as cost-of-living relief and as economic stimulus that channels spending toward local businesses. For 10 points, name this recurring digital payout named for Singapore's five district-level agencies.

This phenomenon was first introduced to Singapore's ride-hailing market by Uber upon its 2013 launch, before five taxi companies including Trans-Cab and Premier Taxi adopted the same system in 2017, and even ComfortDelGro, which once ran an ad campaign boasting it didn't use this practice, capitulated in 2018. Investigations by outlets including the Pulitzer Center found that a leading ride-hailing app's "opaque algorithm" seemed to apply this practice regardless of actual driver availability, undercutting its stated purpose of drawing more drivers onto the road during high demand. Commuters frequently gripe about it kicking in during rainstorms or rush hour, sometimes doubling standard taxi fares. For 10 points, name this demand-driven fare-hiking practice associated with a Southeast Asian ride-hailing "super-app."
answer: Grab surge pricing [or Grab dynamic pricing; prompt on surge pricing or dynamic pricing]

question: A leaked video of this word being chanted at a Nanyang Technological University freshman orientation camp sparked a 2019 investigation after footage showed grown undergraduates repeatedly gesturing toward their crotches while shouting the term. NTU's deputy associate provost for student life said the cheer ran contrary to the university's values of safety, respect, and inclusiveness, and the incident reignited a broader debate about whether Singapore's orientation camps needed an overhaul. Outside of that scandal, the same word appears in children's Singlish as a euphemism for male genitalia, and unrelatedly names a Singapore fashion brand that leaned into the sudden search interest with a "special" promotion. It literally combines a Malay word for a type of fowl with a reduplicated syllable. For 10 points, give this Singlish euphemism whose repeated chanting embarrassed NTU.

Before private catering gradually took over starting in the late 1990s, following considerations that began in 1984, these mess halls were staffed by cooks selected from National Servicemen after Basic Military Training and trained at the School of Army Catering. One soldier recalled a porridge breakfast that "tasted more like a spoonful of salt," while food catered by NTUC was once compared to poison, though quality reportedly improved once other caterers took over. The notorious reputation of meals served here has become a comedic benchmark, invoked whenever Singaporeans want to mock a restaurant or school canteen's food as barely edible. For 10 points, name these communal military dining halls, whose meals are a longstanding punchline in Singapore's National Service folklore.

Singapore's Ministry of Defence has officially dismissed this phenomenon as a myth, stating that its own surveillance shows no increased incidence of respiratory infections among recruits training at the location for which it's named. Despite the official denial, generations of recruits have blamed it on the island's heavily chlorinated water supply drying out throats, on communal living conditions, or on constantly damp clothing and towels in humid barracks. It's named for the island housing Singapore's Basic Military Training Centre, reachable only by ferry from the mainland. Regardless of its disputed medical reality, it persists as a fixture of National Service folklore, with recruits swapping stories about catching it during their first weeks of training. For 10 points, give this dubious ailment named for the island where Singaporean recruits undergo Basic Military Training.

This self-declared "superstar celebrity" first appeared before the Singaporean public at a Singapore Idol audition in 2006, and has since built a reputation on outlandish stunts including getting breast implants in Bangkok, which he removed three years later, and repeatedly posing with WWE championship belts he claims to have won in undisclosed matches. He has cultivated a combative, cyclical relationship with online "haters" who prank him, including one incident where he filed a police report after being fooled into showing up for a fake Mediacorp TV interview. He runs a YouTube channel under his own name with thousands of subscribers and over ten thousand uploaded videos. In April 2026, he was sentenced to over fourteen months in jail for distributing an intimate video of a woman without her consent and for threatening her. For 10 points, name this self-proclaimed Singaporean "superstar celebrity" and internet personality.

This entertainer built one of Singapore's pioneering solo YouTube celebrity channels, amassing over ten million views across a career that has included stints as a Muay Thai competitor, fitness trainer, actor, singer, and dancer. Long after his initial YouTube fame faded, he found a second viral wind on TikTok when a video of him reacting shirtless to a WhatsApp outage, exclaiming its name in a high-pitched voice, blew up among younger Singaporean audiences unfamiliar with his earlier career. He is often affectionately referred to online with a Hokkien term for "older brother" appended to his name. For 10 points, name this Singaporean YouTuber and self-styled entertainer, nicknamed with a Hokkien term for an older brother.

While filing his nomination papers for a Group Representation Constituency during Singapore's 2020 General Election, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat delivered brief remarks that repeatedly stumbled over the constituency's own name without ever clearly stating what he intended to do. His rambling short speech repeatedly promised a proposal for his constituency but was quickly clipped and mocked online. The meme even spawned a charity fundraiser that sold two-dollar stickers bearing the phrase, raising a thousand dollars for charity, while some netizens defended Heng and urged compassion. For 10 points, give this repeated stumbling phrase from Heng Swee Keat's flubbed GE2020 nomination-day speech, referencing a GRC whose name combines a compass point and a shoreline.

At a National Solidarity Party rally in MacPherson SMC on 8 September 2015, this nickname was earned by candidate Choong Hon Heng after he delivered a rambling, Inception-esque analogy involving a handshake and three fingers, culminating in an emphatic declaration before he shouted "Boo! Boo to PAP!" while thumping the podium. The bizarre, confusing rally speech instantly went viral among Singaporean netizens mining General Election 2015 for comic gold. Choong later embraced the nickname with good humor, contesting again in the 2020 election five years after his moment of internet fame. For 10 points, give this nickname earned by NSP candidate Choong Hon Heng for a memorable gesture and catchphrase from his GE2015 rally speech.

Implemented starting 7 April 2020, this policy was initially planned to last until 4 May before being extended to 1 June following continued unlinked community transmission. Under it, non-essential workplaces defaulted to remote work, schools moved to home-based learning, religious gatherings were suspended, and food establishments could offer only takeaway, drive-thru, or delivery service. Its introduction followed the detection of COVID-19 clusters in multiple migrant worker dormitories that came to account for an outsized share of new local cases. Survey respondents ranked socialising, visiting relatives, and exercise as the aspects of daily life it disrupted most. For 10 points, name this electrical-engineering metaphor used as the official name for Singapore's 2020 COVID-19 lockdown.

Seven of this institution's official principles, Loyalty to Country, Leadership, Discipline, Professionalism, Fighting Spirit, Ethics, and Care for Soldiers, were formalized in 1996, with an eighth, Safety, added only in 2013. Yet servicemen have long joked about an unwritten addition summed up as permission to misbehave provided nobody notices. That unwritten addendum reflects entrenched "chao keng" culture, in which National Servicemen evade physically demanding or monotonous duties without their superiors noticing. Reels and memes riffing on it circulate widely on Singaporean social media pages devoted to National Service humor, often listing it right alongside the eight formal principles in a mock-official chart. For 10 points, name this joking extra principle attributed to the Singapore Armed Forces.
answer: (the) SAF's 9th core value [or ninth SAF core value; or don't get caught]

question: Introduced as a pilot scheme on 15 April 2001 covering 2,500 flats across sites in Sengkang and Sembawang, this Housing and Development Board system replaced an earlier registration scheme after the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis left roughly 20,000 unsold flats sitting empty and drew criticism for overestimating housing demand. Under it, prospective buyers select and apply for units at launch sites before construction tenders are called, originally contingent on at least 70 percent of the units being claimed by applicants, a threshold later lowered to 50 percent in 2011. Though its name implies flats are only constructed after customers apply, HDB has since moved toward constructing many of these developments ahead of demonstrated demand. For 10 points, give this abbreviation for Singapore's dominant public-housing sale scheme, under which most Singaporeans apply for and eventually receive a new HDB flat.
